{{Short description|Type of quartic plane curve}}

[[File:Trifolium curve chart.png|thumb|This image shows a trifolium curve using its Cartesian equation.]]

The '''trifolium curve''' (also '''three-leafed clover curve''', '''3-petaled rose curve''', and '''pâquerette de [[The Tale of Melibee|mélibée]]''') is a type of [[quartic plane curve]]. The name comes from the Latin terms for 3-leaved, defining itself as a [[Folium of Descartes|folium]] shape with 3 equally sized leaves.<ref>See also [[trefoil]] arch.</ref> 

It is described as

:<math>
x^4+2x^2y^2+y^4-x^3+3xy^2=0. \,
</math>

By solving for ''y'' by substituting ''y''<sup>2</sup> and its square, the curve can be described by the following function(s):
:<math>
y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{-2x^2-3x\pm\sqrt{16x^3+9x^2}}{2}},\,\,y^2=\frac{-x(2x+3)\pm x\sqrt{16x+9}}{2}
</math>

Due to the separate ± symbols, it is possible to solve for 4 different answers at a given (positive) x-coordinate; 2 y-values per negative x-coordinate. One sees 2 resp. 1 pair(s) of solutions, mirroring points on the curve.

It has a [[polar equation]] of[[File:Three-leaved clover polar.svg|thumb|This image shows the trifolium curve using its polar equation. Its area is equivalent to one quarter the area of the [[inscribed circle]].]]<math> r=-a\cos(3\theta)</math>

and a [[Cartesian equation]] of

<math display="block"> (x^2+y^2)[y^2+x(x+a)] = 4axy^2.</math>

The area of the trifolium shape is defined by the following equation:

<math>A=\frac{1}{2} a^2 \int_{0}^{\pi}\cos^2(3\theta) \, d\theta\,</math><ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Trifolium.html|website=mathworld.wolfram.com|first1=Margherita|last1=Barile|first2=Eric|last2=Weisstein|title=Trifolium Curve Equations}}</ref> <math>=\frac{\pi a^2}{4}</math>

And it has a length of 

<math>6a\int_{0}^{\tfrac{\pi}{2}} \sqrt{1-\frac{8}{9}\sin^2t}\, dt\thickapprox6.7 a</math><ref>{{cite web|url=https://mathcurve.com/courbes2d.gb/trifoliumregulier/trifoliumregulier.shtml|website=mathcurve.com|title=Regular Trifolium|date=2017|first=Robert|last=Ferreol}}</ref>

[[File:Trifolium equations.png|thumb|This image shows two equations for the trifolium defined as <math>x^4+2x^2y^2+y^4-x^3+3xy^2=0</math> (blue) and <math>(x^2+y^2)^3-x(x^2-3y^2)=0</math> (red).]]

The trifolium was described by J.D. Lawrence as a form of [[Kepler's folium]] when

<math>b \in (0, 4, a)</math><ref>{{cite book |last1=Lawrence |first1=J. Dennis |title=A catalog of special plane curves |date=1972 |publisher=Dover Publications |location=New York |isbn=978-0486602882 |url=https://www.amazon.com/exec/obidos/ISBN%3D0486602885/ericstreasuretroA/ |access-date=19 July 2024}}</ref>

A more present definition is when <math display="inline"> a=b.</math>

The trifolium was described by Dana-Picard as 

<math>(x^2+y^2)^3-x(x^2-3y^2)=0</math>

He defines the trifolium as having three leaves and having a triple point at the [[Origin (mathematics)|origin]] made up of 4 [[Arc (geometric)|arcs]]. The trifolium is a [[Algebraic curve|sextic]] curve meaning that any line through the origin will have it pass through the curve again and through its [[complex conjugate]] twice.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dana-Picard |first1=Thierry |title=Automated Study of a Regular Trifolium |journal=Mathematics in Computer Science |date=June 2019 |volume=13 |issue=1–2 |pages=57–67 |doi=10.1007/s11786-018-0351-7 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/326150234 |access-date=19 July 2024}}</ref>

The trifolium is a type of [[rose curve]] when <math>k = 3</math><ref>{{cite web |last=Lee |first=Xah |title=Rose Curve Information |url=https://xahlee.info/SpecialPlaneCurves_dir/Rose_dir/rose.html |website=xahlee.info}}</ref>

[[Gaston Albert Gohierre de Longchamps]] was the first to study the trifolium, and it was given the name ''Torpille'' because of its resemblance to fish<!-- nl: sidderrog/torpedo -->.<ref>{{cite book |last1=de Longchamps |first1=Gaston |title=Cours de Mathématiques Spéciales: Geométrie Analytique à Deux Dimensions |date= |publisher=Nabu Press |year=1884 |isbn=9781145247291 |edition= |location=France |language=fr}}</ref>

The trifolium was later studied and given its name by [[Martyn Cundy|Henry Cundy]] and Arthur Rollett.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Cundy |first1=Henry Martyn |last2=Rollett |first2=Arthur P. |title=Mathematical models |date=2007 |publisher=Tarquin Publications |location=St. Albans |isbn=978-0906212202 |edition=3., repr }}</ref>
